utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Daryl Mundis. We are again assisted today by our intern, Jaspreet Saini, and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to greet everyone present, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused. Before we call the witness into the courtroom, I'd like to inform of the following: The Defence intervened when the Judges were asking some questions. I'd like to point out that when Judges put questions to the witness, as we have already said, Defence may ask questions, put questions to the witness, but after the Judges' questions unless there is a problem with the transcript or unless there is a translation problem. As we are dealing with three languages, B/C/S, French, and English, on a number of occasions, we have noticed that certain problems arise. It's in the transcript that we may know there's a problem. In such a case, you may intervene and ask for the transcript to be corrected. But as far as the substance of the Judges' questions are concerned, neither of the parties should intervene. Rule 46 is very precise. It mentions smooth proceedings, which means that everyone should be allowed to put questions to the witness, and then the parties can ask additional questions if it's necessary to clarify certain issues. If one of the parties is not satisfied or happy with an answer provided by a witness, they may always take the floor again to ask the witness additional questions. I hope we won't have to deal with this issue again. I will now ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom. And I will also provide the Registrar with the documents he requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General. Are you receiving the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I can hear you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a few more questions about three subjects. I will mention them immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They concern the monastery in Guca Gora, then the music school, and finally I will deal with Maline. Then the other Judges will also ask you questions. As far as the Guca Gora monastery is concerned, do you remember how many times you went there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, could you please be more precise as to the period of time you're referring to. Which period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's say in the month of June 1993. Do you remember the number of times that you may have gone to the monastery in June? If you don't remember, I'll try to refresh your memory. Major Kent-Payne, do you remember having met him?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Kent-Payne said that the UN, on the 2nd or 3rd of June, he's not sure of the date, organised a meeting in Guca Gora with the Croatian commander and Colonel Merdan. Do you remember a meeting that took place in Guca Gora at the very beginning of June? He said on the 2nd or 3rd of June, and he added - and if you can't remember this, I'll try and refresh your memory - apparently he said that you said there would be no attack. Do you remember this event?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this event. I went to Guca Gora as a member of the joint command which had its headquarters in Travnik, in the post office building. In addition to myself who represented the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was also a representative of the Croatian Defence Council, Mr. Franjo Nakic. And around that date that you indicated a moment ago, we had a meeting in Guca Gora in the command of the HVO brigade of Guca Gora. This was in the building next to the stadium in Guca Gora. I remember this very well, Your Honours. When Major Kent-Payne quoted me saying what you said I did, I don't exclude the possibility that I said that. I'm sure that the BiH Army during that period of time was not preparing for any attacks. It did not intend to carry out any attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you confirm what he said. Major Kent-Payne said that he went to Guca Gora on the 7th and 8th of June to evacuate the inhabitants. And he said there were 180 inhabitants who were allegedly placed in UN vehicles. Do you know anything about evacuating 180 inhabitants from Guca Gora between the 7th and 8th of June? Were they evacuated in UN vehicles on those dates?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any information about this happening on the 7th or 8th of June, this transport of civilians from Guca Gora. I was present when the evacuation took place. It was on the 9th of June 1993, Your Honours, and I was involved in that evacuation. I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the 9th of June, you were apparently there because there is another witness, Tomislav Rajic who knows you. Do you know him? Because he said, and it's in the transcript, 2830, page 2830, he said that he knew you. Does this name mean anything to you, Tomislav Rajic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know Mr. Tomislav Rajic. I knew him even before I saw him on that day in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he was there in the monastery on the 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you also confirm what he said.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not wish to confirm what he said. I only wish to confirm that I saw him in the monastery on that day. Your Honours, please don't put words into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how we took your testimony. You confirm that you met him on that day.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I do not wish to confirm what he said on that day because I don't know what he said on the day. I know what he told me on that day, Your Honour, and this is what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 13th of June, there were three members of the international community who went to Maline as part of an investigation, that was Mr. Rhode [phoen], Mr. Bower, and Major Kent-Payne. Apparently, they were to have difficulties. It was going to be difficult for them to get there. And having encountered a certain number of difficulties, Major Kent-Payne went to the headquarters of the 3rd Corps to meet General Hadzihasanovic there. And according to this witness, you introduced Mr. Kent-Payne to General Hadzihasanovic, and he then obtained authorisation for free passage, and they were also accompanied by military policemen. Do you remember this event?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this event, Your Honour. I can't remember it at this moment. I do not exclude the possibility that this is how it happened. However, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can't remember this event. Did you hear anything about members of the international community sometimes having difficulties in getting through checkpoints, or did you never receive such information? Because according to this witness, there was a problem.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on several occasions, I did receive information that members of the international community did encounter problems at various checkpoints. And as soon as I received such information, I would go to those checkpoints to deal with the issue. We, from the corps command, never prevented anybody from the international community to move -- from moving freely through the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. I shared with you an example that I witnessed myself. I was there at the checkpoint making sure that representatives of the international community moved freely through a certain checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll move on to the music school now. On the 26th of January 1993, HVO soldiers from Dusina were taken to the music school. Two of these soldiers have testified before this Tribunal. I'll mention the names. One was called Batinic, and another Rados but this certainly won't mean anything to you. But these two witnesses told us that they had been taken to the music school, and they were maltreated there, and one even said that one of the soldiers who was there was called Geler. On the 26th or 27th of January, did you in the 3rd Corps command know that HVO soldiers had been taken to the music school? Were you aware of this event?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I personally was not aware of that. I didn't know that members of the HVO had been taken to the music school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In April, a few months later, other HVO soldiers were also taken to the music school. There are a number of names. A number of soldiers have testified here, and one is called Anto Vrljo, and he said before this Tribunal that someone called Jasmin Isic was in the music school, and another witness called Kruno Rajic said that Jasmin Isic had been on trial, had been sentenced by a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were you aware of the fact that in April, HVO soldiers were in the music school?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I received information from representatives of the international community. They told me that some people had been taken to the music school. I went there with representatives of the international community. We visited the music school. When I was at the music school together with the representatives of the music school, I did not find anything unusual there in the music school. As far as I can remember, the representative of the international community likewise remarked that he did not see anything unusual there. We did not find any incarcerated men there. And, Your Honours, I went to the music school once again around that time because the international community insisted and they kept saying that people were being taken there continuously. I thought that maybe representatives of the international community didn't believe me that there was nobody there. Once I went there unannounced to make sure that I was right, and when I entered the music school unannounced, I still did not see any incarcerated people in the music school. In other words, I never saw anybody who might have been taken to this music school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us the precise dates when you went to the music school? Do you remember them? Or do you remember, roughly speaking, the dates?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was during the period between April and June. It is a rather broad time range. However, I can't give you anything more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One detainee whose name was Kruno Rajic, who was detained from the 23rd of April to the 10th of June, his wife apparently telephoned you and asked you to go to the music school because the 7th Muslim Brigade was there, and apparently you said that the 7th Brigade was not there. That took place over ten years ago. And obviously, it's difficult to remember all the phone calls one received. But do you remember a lady phoning you and mentioning the situation her husband was in in the music school?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I claim with full responsibility that no woman ever called me and asked me to go to the music school. Your Honour, I told you who it was who asked me to go to the music school. I'm sure that it was never a woman. No woman ever asked me to go to the music school on her behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A witness who has testified here mentioned a visit of the Red Cross on the 16th of May 1993. And the witness said that he and two other men were taken to the first floor of the music school, and that is where they saw the Red Cross. But 17 of their comrades had been previously been taken in a van to Bilmiste, and after the end of the Red Cross's visit, they were brought back. That's what he said. What's your opinion of that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any opinion on that because I didn't see it. I can't talk about things I didn't see, Your Honour. I don't have an opinion. I didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a report in evidence from the commission of experts of the Security Council and from the Commission on Human Rights. They date from the end of 1993. In the report of the experts from the Security Council, paragraph 2827 reference is made to the music school and to the fact that people were in the music school. In the report of the Commission on Human Rights, in paragraph 41, reference is also made to the music school. These reports were drafted towards the end of 1993. Did you remain in -- you said that you remained in the 3rd Corps in the course of 1994. When these -- were these reports provided to you? Were you aware of them? Didn't your superior command ask you about the contents of these reports which were internationally known, given the people who had drafted these reports? So first of all, were you aware of these reports? And secondly, did anyone ask you to provide any explanations, any comments on what was contained in these reports?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, whenever the superior command asked the 3rd Corps to provide a report on any of the issues, including this issue, the 3rd Corps command would react. In October, as far as I can remember, I had an opportunity to read requests coming from the Main Staff of the supreme command. They requested from us to draft a report on Maline. We did that, and we sent this report to the superior command. Your Honour, I remember this very well. I do not remember any other requests from the supreme command. They may have arrived. I do not exclude that possibility. I personally don't know whether they did. I was not informed about any of the requests from the supreme command as follow up on these reports that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will enable me to move on to the third and last subject, which is Maline. You said that you were familiar with a letter that someone from the Centre For Human Rights had forwarded to President Izetbegovic. Defence counsel provided this document in its binder. At the same time, we can show you another document, P171. Mr. Registrar, could you show the witness this document. Have a look at the document, but you know the document since Defence counsel has already shown it to you. Rasim Delic sent a letter to the 3rd Corps saying that President Izetbegovic had received this letter in which reference was made to a massacre of 25 Croats in Maline. And naturally, Mr. Delic asked for information, et cetera. This letter arrived in the 3rd Corps, and General Hadzihasanovic immediately sent a letter to the command of the Bosanska Krajina operational group. This is P111, Mr. Registrar. Have a look at P111, a document that you're already familiar with. When you compare the two documents, one notes that General Hadzihasanovic relays all the requests and adds an additional request. So he includes all the requests in this document and adds one additional one. The letter from General Hadzihasanovic dated the 17th of October, were you aware of this letter at the time? Or did you become aware of it at a subsequent date?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was aware of this letter. However, I cannot be specific about the period of time when I learned about this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll show you the last document now, which is P174, because in the last document you yourself actually intervened. I will first check in the B/C/S version that that is, in fact, your signature. Yes, it's your signature. Have a look at the document. And could you confirm that that is, in fact, your signature?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is as follows: This letter was sent on the 21st of October; that is to say, between the 17th and the 21st of October. There is a document we don't have, which is the response from Bosanska Krajina OG to the 3rd Corps. This is missing. It must be somewhere. We don't have the reply from the operational group to the letter dated 17th October from General Hadzihasanovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. When you replied and you signed on the 21st of October, how is it that you signed and not General Hadzihasanovic? Wasn't he there on the 21st of October? Because you see how this was done. The letter was addressed to the president of your country. The president then sent it to the supreme military authority. Then it was forwarded to the 3rd Corps. And you, as number two, replied, and your reply went up the hierarchical chain. So why did you sign on the 21st of October? Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wrote this letter based on the report that we received from our subordinate unit. I know that this is what I based my letter on. I can't give you a proper explanation as to how come I signed this letter at that moment. I can only suppose that at that moment, Commander General Hadzihasanovic was not at the command. Maybe not on that day, or at least not at the time when I was drafting this report. I had already been at the location with the representatives of the international community and Father Stipan. I had seen the place with my own two eyes. I saw where the killed Croats whose number is mentioned here were buried. I cannot be sure why it was signed by me. However, I believe that there were two reasons. The first one is that General Hadzihasanovic was not there and I was. And the second reason is that I had visited this place. I saw the place with my own two eyes. That's why I drafted the report and signed it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the letter, you say that in the course of combat, no civilians were killed by ABiH members, and you also say that no HVO soldiers were executed. And then you say all the Croats were killed as a result of gunshot wounds or as a result of shelling. How do you know that they were killed by bullets or shells? Did you have a report on which you based these claims, or were these just assumptions that you made? Because it says they were -- it says they were killed by bullets and shells. Is this the report from the operational group? Is it in the report from the operational group that this claim was made?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I claim with full responsibility that I drafted this report based on the report from my subordinate unit. I'm sure that in the report of the subordinate unit, it said that in the territory of Maline, there had been combat operations and that during those combat operations, some people were killed. Some members of the HVO. And when we are talking about combat operations, there are two possibilities there. The first one is that a soldier is shot at and hit. And therefore, killed in combat. Or in other words, hit by a bullet from an automatic weapon or some other weapon, or it may be hit by a shell shrapnel. It is a well-known thing how a soldier can get killed during combat. And if that is the report that I received from my subordinate command, that is what I wrote in my report. I'm sure, Your Honour, that in the report that I received from my subordinate unit, it said that these Croats were killed in combat, that they were not murdered by members of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll take the document back, and I will now give the floor to the other Judge who has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. We have been, all those present here, making extraordinary demands on your memory in the past week, and I'm quite amazed of how good your memory is of all those events that took place 10 or 11 years ago. I will continue to put questions which make a call on your good memory, and I will start by putting a few questions on Dusina and only on your travel with the committee, with the commission to the village itself where you met some soldiers in the first place, and then you met some local inhabitants of the village. And I'm referring to your visit in the company of this lady, this Croatian lady, Milica Kegelj. Now, I would like to have -- if possible, a somewhat more sharper idea of your meeting with these Croatian inhabitants in the house of this family of Milica Kegelj. My first question would be how many persons were there? How many persons did you meet in that house?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have already testified about that. I said that I was in a joint delegation up there. I remember Mrs. or Ms. Milica Kegelj who was the interpreter for the European Monitoring Mission as far as I can remember. This is how Milica was introduced to me in any case. With Milica and Mr. Franjo Nakic, I was in a house. Milica told us that the house belonged to their cousins, or maybe it was her house. I can't remember. We entered the house. At that moment, there was nobody in the house. I remember that Milica took some photos from the house, and then we left the house. I was in no other house with Ms. Milica Kegelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But I understood from your testimony a few days ago that you spoke with a number of persons. And I'm not referring to the soldiers you met, but to civilians who lived in the place. That's what I understood --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. I didn't say that I spoke to them in the house. Your question was very precise, and I must say that my biggest problem is the fact that I'm trying to be very precise and very up to point. Sometimes I'm prevented from providing an extensive and complete answer about everything I know. You have asked me about my conversation with Croats in the house in the presence of Ms. Milica Kegelj. I didn't speak to any villagers in the house with Ms. Milica Kegelj. I told you where I was when I spoke with Ms. Kegelj, which house it was. As we were passing through the village, we came across some villagers. I didn't know whether they were Croats, whether they were Bosniaks. I didn't ask what their ethnic origin or religious background was. We were looking for the local commander of Dusina, and we spoke to him. That is how I have testified, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: It shows how easy it is to make mistakes. I spontaneously assumed that you have met -- had met these persons in the house of the family of that lady. But that is apparently not the case. So when speaking with these people you met in Dusina, this was in the streets somewhere? How many people did you meet?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a path, a very steep path. There was a lot of people there. We were passing through, and I can't remember how many people we spoke to. In any case, there were a lot of people. Together with Franjo Nakic, I tried to find a local commander which was the only logical thing to do for a soldier. When we found the local commander, we talked to him. I can't remember his name. He informed us what had happened on the previous days in Dusina village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: We've had the local commander a few weeks ago or a few days ago before you came. And basically, he said the same as you said last week, that there were -- that there had been fights, and that he assumed that these persons were killed during fight. So I understand that both Nakic and you were putting questions to some of the people who were present in the group of persons that you met. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, when you talked for the first time about this meeting, part of a report was read out to you. And it quotes what Mr. Fleming, the member of the European Observers has said. He said the following, I'll read it again to you: "We visited the town of Busovaca and witnessed the consequences. It was sad. The inhabitants were frightened and desperate, and in Lasva, Dusina," he said, "it was difficult not to feel that something terrible had taken place." And then he continues saying: "The citizens there did not give any sign of noticing anything or did not dare to." And I was struck by the last sentence "the citizens there did not give any sign of noticing anything or did not dare to." So if I understand this well, but please correct me if I'm wrong, both of you were putting questions but not getting any answers. Is that a correct interpretation of this phrase?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that we received from the local population talked about combat operations and casualties. I did notice that these people were frightened. It was the first time in the lives of these people to be subject to combat operations in their vicinity. For the first time, they saw their fellow villagers being killed in combat. This is a shock for any human being when a neighbour sees their neighbours being killed. I don't know whether you, Your Honour, have ever had an opportunity to see or witness that. But I assure you, these are the most difficult moments in the life of any one person. They were frightened. We were all frightened. We were all afraid of war, of dying, of being killed. And these people were really terrified, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. The people you met --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to seek clarification. I have a report here quoting Mr. Fleming, but this is a report that was drafted by Mr. Nakic. I don't know whether this is the report that you're referring to because when you were conveying Mr. Fleming's words and when you said that these people had not shown any sign or didn't dare say anything, the reference is made to Busovaca rather than to Dusina. So I don't know whether you're referring to this report or to some other report. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You understand this as having regard to Busovaca and not to Dusina itself. Well, this is maybe a matter of debate. You could argue that this has regard to Lasva and Dusina also. But I note that you think it's only about Busovaca. I read it as having regard to Lasva and Dusina also. But I'm mainly interested -- yes, it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was just to confirm whether we are talking about the same document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But I hope that I have quoted the text correctly. Would you concede that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. I did not understand because you mentioned that these words were conveyed by Mr. Nakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you yourself read it out in the first questions you put -- the Defence put on the meeting in Lasva. Anyhow, I'm interested in your own observations. And this was only to put to you questions on what you saw and what you heard.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was very precise, and I provide you with a detailed answer as to what I saw during my stay because this is what you asked me, and I believe that I've given you very precise information as to what I heard from these people and what I heard from the local commander. I didn't hear anything else, Your Honour. And all I can do is just repeat what I've already testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So let me continue asking you about your meetings with the population in Lasva. You said there were Croats, there were Bosnians, there were quite a lot of people. You spoke to some of them. And my next question is: Did you also meet persons who were eyewitnesses to the fighting, apart from the commander that we have already spoken about? I understand that most villagers have an impression of hearing firearms and -- but were there any direct eyewitnesses of the fighting itself? Could you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't even know whether the local commander participated in combat or not. I never asked him that. I never asked anybody whether they were involved in combat directly. Your Honour, I really did not ask that on that day. I didn't ask anybody about that in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And were there, among the persons present at that moment, were there any persons that you might consider to be able to have taken part in the fighting? I mean, were there men there of fighting age, not too old to have potentially participated in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw some able-bodied men there. I also saw men in uniform. People were passing through Dusina in the direction of Busovaca Municipality because this was at the time the only way for some of the people from Busovaca to go to Zenica. For a while, this was a very busy road. I saw able-bodied men passing through the village. Your Honour, you have to be aware of the fact that in the area of Busovaca at that time, there was still a lot of area under the control of the BiH Army and that the only way people from Busovaca could go to Zenica was by way of this road. There was no other road. I've already told you that the main road had been blocked, had been mined by the HVO. A lot of people moved through that village every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: How long did your stay last there? Was it one hour, 15 minutes, two hours? Can you give an indication how long you have been there.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I want to be as precise as possible, I believe that I was there between one and two; not longer. An hour, two hours. We didn't stay less than an hour there, but no longer than two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You spent that time talking to persons who you met?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm taking into account our travelling through the village. I told you that this was a very difficult road to negotiate for the vehicles. The road was very steep, very difficult to negotiate. We did not spend two hours talking to the villagers. We spent maybe 15 minutes to half an hour talking to the villagers. But all in all, it took us about two hours to go through the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... considerably for me. A few moments ago, it was said that some of the Croat persons who had participated in the fight were taken prisoners and brought to the music school in Zenica. There was a discussion on your visits to the music school. I still have one question, and I'm putting this question because we heard earlier testimony from international witnesses. When inspecting the school together with the international observers or when on other occasions you yourself alone went to the school, I assume that you inspected the whole building from top to bottom, so to speak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Whatever they wanted to see, whatever the representatives of the international community wanted to see, they were able to see in my presence. I don't know whether the international community representatives had any other opportunity to go there in my absence. I don't know. I'm only telling you what I know. Once, when I went to the music school unannounced to dispel the suspicion of the international community that the 3rd Corps was hiding something from the international community with regard to the music school, I again inspected all the rooms, and I did not find any incarcerated soldiers of the HVO or civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The basement as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You also spoke about Miletici. I'm not going to ask you any questions of substance on that event. But I have one very minor question, so to speak, maybe even silly, but it arose yesterday when this was again discussed. A document was quoted to you, and it says -- I'll have a look. This is P148. A Brit -- a European Union report, and it reports the statements of local persons as having observed persons with police badges on their shoulders, including a triangle. And I'm not going to ask you whether this observation was right or wrong or whether they were mistaken or correct. But I only want to know the following. Out of my ignorance of the situation in Bosnia at the time, if I would have met in 1993 in Zenica or elsewhere a person with a badge and a triangle in it, would that indicate? Would that be some form of police or whatever?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't answer that question. I don't know whether such a person would have been a policeman or not. I'm familiar with the official insignia worn by ABiH members. There are various types of insignia. Men who wore various types of uniforms wore various types of insignia. The international community had various types of insignia. Perhaps you could have come across such a person wearing a triangle, having such a badge. But I don't know what it would have meant. Your Honours, there were a lot of insignia worn by individuals in the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility. So it is possible that there was such insignia, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... such a badge.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I never saw such a triangle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, let's go to Maline. I have more questions to put to you on the events in Maline. At the beginning of your testimony, you said that you heard the first information about the murders -- "first information about the murders reached me from the international community. And as ever I reacted immediately. I suggested that we should go there in order to investigate what kind of murders or killings had taken place. And where they were presented to us by the international community." This is a quote of what you said on the 9th of December last week. Yesterday, I have not been able to note it down, but yesterday you said what exactly happened in Maline only became clear to me when I was a witness in the Kordic and Cerkez case, and I found this a very interesting remark. What did you hear in the Kordic and Cerkez case, if it was that case because you have also been a witness in another case, isn't it? But my question is: What did you hear in that case? Because it was new to you, you said.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was all new to me at the time. When I heard that crimes had been committed up there, that was new to me. When I heard that foreigners had committed these crimes, well, this was information that was new to me, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honours. Because up until then I had information that there had been combat in that area up there, and that members of the HVO had been killed in the course of the combat. But when I heard that crimes had been committed by foreigners, I was very surprised by this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... who told you that? Do you remember? Was it the Defence in that case?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember right now. I don't know whether this took place when I was being proofed for my testimony in the Kordic case, or perhaps it was in the course of the Prosecution's or Defence's case. I really can't remember now, Your Honours. I don't remember when I was told that these crimes were committed by foreigners up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You told us that you went with a European observer, Mr. Landry, and the person Stipan Radic to Maline in the beginning of August. And my question is -- you visited Maline also, the three of you. And my question to you is: Did any of them, either Mr. Remy Landry or Mr. Stipan Radic, enter into details about the murders that could have been taken place there? Did they add something to that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't rule out that possibility. I know what we asked the soldier, the soldier who took us to the site where these people who had been killed were buried. The soldier told us that people who had been killed in combat were buried there. I don't know whether Mr. Remy asked any -- put any specific questions to the soldier who took us there, or perhaps Mr. Stipan did that. But I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking this because you don't go for nothing to Maline. If you go to Maline in the company of an international observer and a Croatian priest who want to be there, who want to go there, there must be a reason that -- there must be a reason saying that something unusual has happened. And I'm asking you, did either the European observer or the Croatian priest give you some more information, apart from saying there have been killings or something like that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that representatives of the international community and the priest, Stipan Radic, said that they suspected that something like that may have happened. But they didn't say that the murder had been committed. They just said that they suspected that this might have occurred. They wanted me to take them to the site so they could see that. And when the soldier who took us there told us that men who had been killed in combat were buried there, we really didn't look into the case. We didn't investigate it. At least not on my level. Quite a few men had been killed in combat by that time. You mentioned a number of over 500. If we investigated -- if we had investigated all of those cases, we would have needed a lot of time. At that point in time, I really couldn't investigate the matter. We only went to see what the situation was as such a suspicion did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My next question, do you remember having been visited by a person on behalf of the United Nations in September 1993? The United Nations had an investigator, and he wrote a report in which he mentioned that he had met you in September 1993, and that he -- you discussed -- you two discussed the matter of Maline together. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had a lot of meetings in various locations with representatives of the international community. Could you perhaps refresh my memory, refer to a specific meeting, so that I can answer your question more precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... do you remember that name?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't really remember it. I wouldn't exclude the possibility of having met this gentleman, too. It's difficult for me to remember all the meetings I had with all the representatives of international organisations who passed through the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility in the course of a year or throughout the period that I was in the 3rd Corps, which was for over two years. A lot of people passed through the zone. I wouldn't rule out the possibility of meeting this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I can imagine that. But let's look at the report itself, there's a summary, a description of a conversation with you. And I think in the B/C/S version, this would be page 5. And in the English version, it is page -- it starts on page 3. Have you found the page there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, everything is in English. And I don't understand English. So it's difficult for me to find my bearings here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He should be shown the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have page 5 of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you may note that this seems to be a summary of a meeting this person had with you in Zenica on the 23rd of September. And in the second linea, you may read that he is asking you for permission to visit the village of Maline where reportedly 25 Croat civilians had been massacred on the 8th of June. That is the first sentence of that linea. I will not read the following text, but he is apparently asking you for permission to go there, and you answer him: There's no need for me to give you permission. You can go all by yourself or ask the local commanders for permission. If you want to read that, go ahead. I'm just summarising what is said in this part of the text.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. That's what it says in this paragraph. As Mr. Kiril says, this part of the text says that the general policy of the 3rd Corps command is not to provide written authorisation because people have the right to move round freely unless someone from the international community insisted on having such permission we wouldn't give such an authorisation. And on a number of occasions I have said that if someone from the international community could not reach a certain destination, I would go to the location, to the site, and try and resolve the difficulty. There were security problems at the front lines alone. No one could guarantee your security there. The local commanders were in the best position to know whether there was combat in their area. And yesterday, I said that the corps command had an overview of what was happening in the field at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... permits and freedom to travel and respect for international organisations. I just mentioned this to help you remember the meeting itself. Do you remember having had this conversation with the man? Maybe you don't. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Then he -- let's skip the next linea and read the following two lineas which are again on Maline, at least. Well, the first of them is Maline. Could you read them to us.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, are you referring to the following paragraphs "in the area under the control of the 3rd Corps"? Is that the paragraph you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm referring to the linea that starts in B/C/S with "Vracajuci se u Maline." It's on the bottom half of page 5. Can you find it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's not the following paragraph, it's two paragraphs further down. I'll read it. "On returning to Maline, he explained that usually after combat, the area was cleaned up. The dead would be buried. The corpses of animals would be burnt, et cetera. In the vicinity of Maline, there are two mass graves in which between 25 and 30 individuals have been buried." And he is not able to say how many civilians there are among them. End of quote, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I was asking you to read it mainly because it might refresh your memory again. Do you now remember having met this person, or is it still lost in your memory? And again, if you don't remember, I can't blame you. That is...

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I still have a very hazy recollection of these details. I can't remember these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Could you now read the next linea of this report, the following linea.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In response to my answer on the issue of the mujahedin, he explained that there were no mujahedin units in the ABiH, but that there were a lot of volunteers from various countries. And there were westerners among these volunteers. They had come to "fight against the contemporary form of fascism, and they were all expected to abide by the laws of the ABiH." End of quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you have read this part of the report, too, do you now remember the meeting? Or is it still lost in your memory?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that on two or three occasions when speaking to representatives of the international community, I said that there were no mujahedin units in the ABiH. But I said that there were volunteers from various countries. Your Honours, you must understand that there were people from various countries in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the beginning of the Army [as interpreted], the army commander wasn't a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but nevertheless he was the commander of the ABiH. I was referring to those volunteers who became engaged in the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those are the foreigners I had in mind, and not the armed foreigners. When the Prosecution put their questions to me, we provided a -- we gave a very strict definition of the term "armed foreigners." I accepted to call them the mujahedin, but then in whatever I say, we'll be saying that they are mujahedin. I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... your conversation, but apparently you don't remember the conversation with this person, so I will put no further questions about it. But it has to do with the report of the United Nations that you -- that was sent later on to the army and on the basis of which you made your own report. That's why I am discussing this document with you.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, if I may make a comment. I didn't draft my report on the basis of this report. I didn't have the opportunity of seeing this earlier report. The report I drafted wasn't on the basis of the request contained in this report. I think it was on the basis of a request made by someone else. I'm not sure if I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... suggest that you used this in this text. I only said that this report was at the basis -- or I wanted to say that this report was at the basis of the request of the United Nations to give more information. The reason why the United Nations asked for information to the Bosnian Army is partly based on this report and other things he wrote to his superior, Mr. Mazowiecki, the Polish gentleman. But I did not in any way suggest or wanted to suggest that this report was at the basis of your report in the sense that you had made use of it. That's not my purpose. So let's go to your own report, and you have been given a binder by the Defence that it may be useful to give you again. I see it's time for a break. And I leave you with this material for the break. And if you want to consult it, go ahead. We will come back in some minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have our break now. It's half past 10.00, and we'll resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: We were busy dealing with the events in Maline, Witness, and I realise now that my questioning to you may make -- may require more time than I expected, and maybe we should increase the tempo of our exchanges a little bit. What I would like to ask you is to -- not to resume -- repeat things you already said because we all know what you said. Only if you think I'm misunderstanding you or I misunderstood you in the past few days, please don't hesitate to answer. But if that is not the case, don't repeat what you have already said, because we all know, and this may perhaps increase the speed of our exchanges. Is that all right with you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will abide by your rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to turn now to your own report of the 21st of October. You have received this binder that the Defence used in the previous days to discuss with you Maline. You have it before you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I turn to your own report, I would like to ask you a few other questions. The first is the following: I suppose you know the former commander in the ABiH Army in 1993, Fikret Cuskic. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I know Mr. Fikret Cuskic. He is currently a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me tell you that he has been testifying before you came, and this was on the 9th of December. So some two -- no, no, this is your testimony. I'm sorry. That was on the 22nd of November of this year. And he said something about Maline that I would like to read to you. He said the following, on page 12.001 of the transcript, about Maline: "One soldier told me that he had information according to which a group of HVO members had been kidnapped by the mujahedin, and rumour had it that they had been killed. Since I knew that Commander Alagic wasn't informed about this, I think he was in Krpeljici at the time, I bypassed that chain of command, and I provided a letter to the corps commander. I was quite categoric in that letter. I was quite severe because I was seriously affected by this information." His remarks were made within the framework of an exhibit presented by the Defence, and that exhibit was a response of the commander of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Hadzihasanovic, to his letter. And that response has the name of 20 of June of 1993. I'm now referring to Defence Exhibit 1224. Maybe you could have a look at it, if the Registrar could produce the document. Have a look at it and give me a sign when you are ready, reading it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've looked at the document, and I have read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have two questions about this document of this exchange of letters. The first is: When you prepared your report in October after the supreme command staff asked for a report, were you aware of this exchange of letters? Was that among the information you had? I'm asking this because you said before in the beginning of your testimony last week "when I wrote my report on the events in Maline, I had at my disposal what I heard and saw during our visit to Maline, together with the international observer and the Croatian priest, and my other source of information was the report that I received from Mr. Delic," which is also in the binder and which you made a reference to. So I assume, having heard you saying that, that you were not aware of this exchange of letters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I said that we had different information, and what was written on the 10th was written in October 1993. I can see that this letter was part of the exchange between the brigade commander and the commander of the 3rd Corps, and that this was -- this happened in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. But my only question is, when you were asked to write your report for the United Nations eventually, you were not aware of these documents, these two letters? That is, the letter of Mr. Cuskic to the commander of the 3rd Corps, and the answer? They were not given to you by some librarian or some other person?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I asked for my subordinate unit to draft the report and send it to me when I received it I drafted my report based on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the response. If you look at the second line, the second sentence of the report, it does say the following: "An investigation into the events in the village of Maline has been launched." I'll stop there. Were you aware of the existence of an earlier investigation when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have already testified that the corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic, asked for this problem to be solved. As far as I can remember, I have already spoken about that. I was not aware of the operative measures that had been taken with regard to this event. I wrote my report based on the report that I received from my subordinate unit on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the day when the report was requested by the supreme command staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I'm not suggesting that there was an earlier investigation or that it was different from the investigation on which you received a report a few days before you made your own report. That is a matter that we will discuss with other witnesses. That has no significance at this moment, but I only wanted to know whether you were aware of this exchange of letters and what has been said in them. Now, let's now turn to the report that you received from Mr. Delic. That is one of the sources of your report, your own report. This is number 4 of your binder, and the exhibit is DK17. It's not Drina Corps, it's DK17. Seventeen, not 70. Now it's right, okay. Do you have before you number 4? No, it's number 5. I apologise. It's number 5. It's my mistake. I mean the report by Delic, Rasim. Do you have it? All right.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have this document before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Since I'm not sure that the last sentence of this report is properly translated into English, I would like to read you the last sentence of this report for all of us. Could you do that, read the last sentence of the report.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last sentence reads: "We would like to point out that all persons were killed during combat." End of quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking this because the translation we have in the English version says -- uses the word "reminds," and you now said in the English translation "to point out." That might make a difference. That's why I asked you to read it. Now, coming to your own report, Witness, this is number 6 in your binder. And it is also Exhibit P174. You said before that your report on the events of Maline were based on your trip to Maline together with Landry and Radic, and on the report of Rasim Delic that we have looked at a few moments ago. Your report is also about other matters that are not of relevance to us at this moment, other events. The last part of your report is especially devoted to Maline. And I think what is said there reflects what you told -- basically reflects what you told about your sources of information. I would like you to pay attention to the third linea of your report. Could you please read it out to us.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the text that I have before me is illegible. It's very difficult for me to read it. Do you have a more legible version of this text? I'm finding it very difficult to read this copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do my best, and I can try and read it. It's really very difficult to read from the copy that I have before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I totally understand your difficulty. I can hardly read it myself. Maybe there's a better copy, or otherwise I will read it in the English text and will ask you whether this is a true reflection of what you wrote. But maybe there is a better copy here. It's always a problem. We all seem to have the same bad copy, so maybe I could read out the translation to you. Maybe you could follow the copy, and this would possibly help you in reading the original text. Let me read the English translation for you then. It says: "Soldiers of the [illegible]," I think it's the 306th Brigade, "soldiers of the [illegible] and armed citizens who were not members of the BH Army units and who obtained weapons through some private channels took part in the combat actions in the region of the village Maline." That is the English text. Have you found it? Can you read --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot see this in this copy. The copy is very bad. Your Honour, please bear this in mind. Yesterday, I found myself in very difficult positions when there were misunderstandings in the translation of particular words. Some of the words of my language could not be interpreted properly into English. I don't know whether I understood what you read, and I don't know whether this is the true reflection of the B/C/S text before me. I would kindly ask you to provide me with a text that I can, (a), understand in my language and that I can, (b), read easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right. That would be the proper thing to do. I agree with you if you cannot read your original. So we'll have to ask, I think, the Prosecutor to provide us with a -- the original. That must be stored somewhere, and there's a special procedure for making it available. Maybe I could continue with you on the basis -- you have it in your possession? That's great. Are you able to read it in the original? Or is that as bad as the copy?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is easier for me to read this original version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So if you're able to read it, albeit with difficulty, would you please read the third linea that I have read before.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will read the third paragraph. "Soldiers of the 306th Mountain Brigade and armed villagers who were not members of BH Army units and who had obtained weapons through some of the private channels took part in the combat actions in the region of Maline." End of quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have two questions about this part of your report. The first is the following: This is information about villagers who were not members of the BH Army units that I suppose, but maybe I'm mistaken, was not information that was provided by Landry and Radic, or was obtained in the report of Rasim Delic. It seems to be outside the scope of what you heard from those sources. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it says very clearly that in the general sector of Maline village, there was combat, and that this happened in that general sector. As an officer and a military professional, I know that with one mentions the general sector of Maline, that doesn't refer only to the village itself. Let me explain, Your Honour. During the same period when the fighting took place, in the second paragraph of my letter, it says "at the beginning of June 1993." After that, there's the paragraph that you singled out and asked me to read. I knew from the report that had arrived during that period in the command of the 3rd Corps that there had been combat operations in the general area of Maline village. I have already testified at great length about the situation that prevailed in these villages in early June 1993. So when you look at the second paragraph and the third paragraph after that as a sequence to the second paragraph, you may conclude that this covers a longer period and a broader area surrounding the village of Maline. As a professional, when it comes to drafting reports, I could not just copy the report that I had received from my subordinate command because my superior officer would think of me as lacking skills and professionalism in my job. I have already mentioned on several occasions that our reports were often drafted by people who lacked skills, who were not professionals, who had not completed military education. I knew that this report of mine was very important and of very general operative significance, and that is why I drafted it the way I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand that. This line on armed citizens who were not members of BH Army units is something you added yourself on information you yourself possessed. It is not from Landry or from Radic, nor is it from the report of Delic? But you said "I have other information at my disposal, and I may use that in writing my report." I understand that. But then my next question is: Why do you mention "armed citizens who were not members of the BH Army units and who obtained weapons through private channels"? Why mention that? What is the relevance of that? If there has been a fight and people have been killed during the fight as a consequence of the fight, what is the relevance of this remark, your remark?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to answer your question very clearly, in order to be fully understood, one must understand what the situation was like during the period referred to here. The date is the 21st of October, but the report has to do with a broader context, and I've already testified about this. During this period, we didn't have a unified command of the 306th Brigade. The command of the 306th Brigade was crying out for help. It was in a hopeless position. I wanted to demonstrate the complexity of the situation at the time. It wasn't only ABiH members who had been attacked there. But the inhabitants, the villagers were attacked, too. The villagers mounted a defence themselves until the command of the 306th Brigade managed to link up and before the 306th Brigade obtained assistance from outside. The situation was chaotic, and I'm referring to a longer period of time than this report. I'm not only referring to a precise date, to the 8th of June 1993, because the superior command requested that I provide a more general report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did it happen in the region of Maline in that period, that armed civilians took part in fights? That would be contrary to any military procedure, I would think. Armed civilians take part; that is against the rule of war, I would say.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with you, but the inhabitants were attacked and they were defending themselves, Your Honour. Your Honour, at that time, our army wasn't strong enough to defend the people in all areas. I have testified about this in very precise terms. So it's quite normal to expect that when the population is attacked, they will defend themselves as the army can't defend them. But there's no military logic to such cases if you have a well-equipped army. But if you know how the army or rather the 3rd Corps was equipped and armed, then, Your Honour, there's a lot of logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And you're saying also -- I'm sorry. You're saying also that this is not something that happened in Maline only, but also in other parts of Central Bosnia other times. Was this quite a regular occurrence, that armed civilians took part in fighting by the army?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agree that it's not logical for civilians to engage in fighting. It's logical for soldiers to fight. I fully agree with your position. But you must bear in mind the specific situation in which this occurred. In other areas, when villages were attacked, the inhabitants of those villages would defend themselves until the arrival of the army. But when the troops arrived and organised themselves to defend the village, then they would take over the defence of that village. So this was not only characteristic of Maline. In practice, this occurred in other places and at other times when it was necessary for the population to defend themselves, not only in the area of the 3rd Corps but throughout the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I still have a question on that because as I understand, but I may be mistaken, but as I understand the events in Maline on the 8th of June, the attack was from the BH Army. So Maline was, if I remember well, not attacked by HVO forces, but on the contrary. There was an attack by the BH Army. So I don't see how you can speak about civilians defending their towns or villages.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must remind you of something. At the beginning of June, I was a member of the joint command that had its headquarters in the post office in Travnik. The information that arrived at that joint command -- well, there were representatives of the HVO, and sometimes there were international monitors, and according to information we obtained, there were shells that had been fired from the upper part of the village of Maline where the majority of the population was Croatian. And they shelled the lower part of the village of Maline inhabited by Bosniaks, the majority was Bosniak in that part of the village. These were provocations. Naturally, this affected the way events unfolded. But according to information I had before the 8th of June, there was information that the Bosniak part of the village had been shelled, which is below the part of the village inhabited by Croats or where Croats form the majority. So when you go to the place, when you see the position of the village -- of these two parts of the village, then you can say that the lower part of the village was under greater threat than the upper part of the village. I'm referring specifically to the village of Maline now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But I note that the letter of Delic as well as the request for submission of data by Hadzihasanovic specifically speak about the 8th June -- July, they say, but this must be June of 1993, not on the days before, not on the days after, it's the 8th of June. And as far as I know, but I may be mistaken, on the 8th of June, the ABiH Army took Maline.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. Members of the ABiH liberated Maline on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So that is where my question comes from. If that is the case, why mention armed civilians with regard to the events of the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a professional, I linked up the paragraphs you have referred to. I only read out the third paragraph. I didn't read out the second paragraph. The following paragraphs were based on the second paragraph or followed on from the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So to resume our discussion on this point, are you stating in the report that there were civilians engaged in an attack on Maline on the 8th of June, or are you not stating that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mentioned the wider area, the general sector of the village of Maline because I didn't have precise information as to whether ABiH members were engaged in combat in Maline along with the civilian population. I did not have such precise information on the 8th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Regarding your reports of the 17 October, you, of course, saw the request for information by General Hadzihasanovic. I suppose you also had received a copy of the letter of Rasim Delic? These are number 3 and 4 of your binder. My question is: Were you also provided at the time that you had to write your report with a copy of the letter of the United Nations itself or a translation of it? Because I understand you did not speak English, read English. Were you provided by the superior commanders or by the government with a translation of the letter of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the superior command, or rather supreme command staff only provided me with this document from the supreme command staff. I didn't receive the original letter from the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina or from international organisations, nor did I receive a translation at the time. I only had the document from the supreme command staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right. Let me explain why I'm asking you this. If you read -- there's no need to do that now, but if you would read the original letter of the United Nations, you would see that there's a reference to mujahedin. And there is no mention of that any more in the letter of Delic and the request of Hadzihasanovic. But in your report, you speak about armed civilians with their own weapons and one might be tempted to think there is a connection between the two, that you are, in fact, making a reference to mujahedins. That's why I asked you all these questions. Are you able to follow my reasoning?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am able to follow your reasoning very well. I have already testified about this to a certain extent. The first time with, let's call them armed foreigners, let's say they were the mujahedin, occurred after the 9th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I think you would now repeat your testimony of the previous days. But since you make a reference to armed civilians, and since the original letter of the United Nations mentions mujahedin, I was simply asking you whether this would be understood, this part of your letter, to be a reference to mujahedin. And if you say "I was not aware of the presence of mujahedin until much later," then I accept that as your testimony. But read in isolation, you could think that your letter, in fact, refers to mujahedin. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the letter from the supreme command staff, I didn't come across the word "the mujahedin." So I did not have the letter from Mr. Mazowiecki, and I couldn't have answered in precise terms as Mr. Mazowiecki had requested. As a soldier, I tried to provide precise answers to the questions put to me by my superior command. And I think that as far as that is concerned, I was very successful in answering these questions precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Maline I wanted to discuss with you. Let's now turn to the large issue of the foreign fighters that you have been discussing with the Defence as well as with the Prosecutor. Before we do that, I'm sorry, I still have some questions, very few questions on another aspect of the events in Central Bosnia in 1993 which is related to the larger question of foreign fighters but has regard specifically to one aspect of the indictment, and that aspect deals with events in Travnik in October 1993. And I'm asking you questions about that because, first of all, this may have to do with foreign fighters; and secondly, your name has been mentioned in a document that I found in the matter. Let me put you my questions. In October 1993, some Croat persons were kidnapped in the city of Travnik and taken to somewhere else. The allegation in the Indictment is that one of these persons has been beheaded in a certain camp And that this was done by members of the -- of mujahedin subordinated to the battle group Bosanska Krajina. I don't want to discuss the whole matter with you, but I'll only ask you a few questions. The first is that in a report that has the number P226, BritBat is mentioning your name in respect to these events. And what is said is the following. One of the officers of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. BritBat has apparently spoken with you, and he relates that "the 3rd Corps had tasked Alagic, commander of the operational group Bosanska Krajina, to resolve the ongoing problems with the mujahedin in Travnik." This may have been the commander itself, Alistair Duncan. I'm not quite sure. But do you remember having said to a member of BritBat that Alagic was charged by the 3rd Corps to solve the problems of -- the ongoing problems with the mujahedin in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember that event very precisely. This occurred in October. I have testified about this at length. I remember that around that time, we issued an order stating that the El mujahedin detachment should be subordinated - not subordinated, resubordinated, the difference is important - to the Bosanska Krajina OG. At the time, the commander of the Bosanska Krajina OG was General Alagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... was this a British officer? Do you remember having said this to this person?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it depends on how I was quoted in that report. I know that the problem of the mujahedin was a serious problem, and that General Alagic could not solve it. It was a problem that wasn't solved at the highest level. I was in the 3rd Corps, and there were problems in 1994 with the El mujahedin detachment, too. And that report, it was probably paraphrased, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: May we not assume that you were aware of the kidnappings of a number of Croats in Travnik in October, or weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And how would you explain this quote? Let me read it full to you again. "Commander first PWO" - I think this is Alistair Duncan - "spoke with General Merdan deputy commander of the 3rd Corps BH, BHO, who made the following unsubstantiated points: (B) that 3rd Corps had tasked Alagic commander operation group Bosanska Krajina to resolve the ongoing problems with the mujahedin in Travnik." I can imagine you're not aware any more of that meeting, but it is difficult for me to accept that he is not telling the truth or that he is not representing correctly what happened.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I can claim with full responsibility that Duncan Alistair never told me that some Croats had been kidnapped in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me quote then from the transcript of Alistair Duncan who has been a witness here on the 13th of May 2004. It is the French transcript, and it is page 7.269. I'll translate it to you in English. "I remember one occasion on which Dzemal Merdan did -- that he instructed Alagic to settle the question of the mujahedin in Travnik."
