utterances.text: I'm just asking you, what do you think of the document? What does it indicate? What does it not indicate? How do we have to understand the document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this document, it being what it seems, sent from Donji Vakuf to the commander of the 3rd Corps with Selmo Cikotic indicated at the bottom, then I can say that this document, written as it is, was sent from Donji Vakuf -- Gornji Vakuf, sorry, to the command of the 3rd Corps requesting that one man be taken from Lendo to be sent to the village of Bistrica where he should get by the morning, and take over command of what is probably an infantry company from Novi Travnik. Furthermore, it says also of the mujahedin and the troops from Bistrica. And then the axis of the attack is indicated, as I read before.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note: PDO means anti-sabotage detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... in this text, what are you thinking about. What is your association with that word in this context?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means to me that this man who wrote this, or as you said yourself, if it is not necessarily Selmo Cikotic. Anyway, the person who wrote this obviously has information that there are mujahedin in the vicinity of Gornji Vakuf. It doesn't say exactly how many or which unit they're in. But I read this as meaning that there are in the broader locality of Gornji Vakuf some mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But it is also a request to order Lendo, a certain Lendo, to do something with -- to take over command of persons among which apparently there are mujahedin. And that is what I want to know. How do you understand this phrase?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my thoughts run in a somewhat different direction. What is requested here is that Lendo assign a man or give a man, not that Lendo himself goes someplace, but that Lendo assigns a person who will go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I think you're right there, but that is maybe a minor aspect. Whoever goes there, Lendo himself or some other person, someone has to take command over people, including, as the text says, mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I fully agree with you. This is what is stated in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, my -- I'm sorry. My question is who are they? Have you any idea? Are these the foreign soldiers, these other people?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no information to that effect. Therefore, I cannot answer your question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move quickly to the last topic I want to discuss with you as briefly as I can. That is the exchange of -- yes, exchange of prisoners in the month of May. HVO soldiers, HVO officers against foreign persons. We have already discussed this at length, but I have only a few aspects to discuss with you. I understand from what you said and from what I have seen from other witnesses, that you were involved in effecting the exchange on behalf of the army. You were offering assistance in the whole operation. I also heard you saying that at a given moment in time, you went together with international observers to Ravno Rostovo, from Travnik to Ravno Rostovo. You inspected a site, a hotel, where the HVO said four officers were, you found nothing, and you went back to Travnik. The same story as you told us has been told by an international observer called Lars Baggesen. Do you know him? Do you remember his name, Scandinavian military man?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to acquaint you with my thoughts concerning my testimony so far about the exchange of the HVO officers who had been kidnapped. You may have said - I don't know because I don't understand English - however, the interpreter interpreted to me as though I participated in the exchange operation. Your Honour, I never participated in the entire exchange operation. Your Honour, I gave testimony here saying that I only participated in what took place in Travnik, not in the entire exchange operation. Your Honour, I was the army representative for Travnik only, and that was only the minor portion of the exchange operation. Therefore, I do not appreciate being said something that I did not give testimony about. This is very important for me. I cannot agree with you that I participated in the entire operation because I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. You have told us about Travnik, and I considered that as a form of cooperation in solving the problem. And I do not want to imply more, but maybe I was not careful enough in phrasing my remarks. But I don't want to talk about the whole operation, only about Travnik and your visit to Ravno Rostovo. And I asked you whether you went together among others with Lars Baggesen, if you remember that name.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour. The question, once again, was not specific enough for me. I did meet with Mr. Lars Baggesen. However, when I went to Rostovo, which you have mentioned, or at least the interpreter has interpreted that to me, I stated that I went to Ravno Rostovo with European monitors, which was prior to the exchange of the kidnapped HVO officers. I went to Ravno Rostovo with the representatives of the European Monitoring Mission. Their leader was Juan Valentino. He was the leader of that visit. I was present there with Franjo Nakic. We were searching for the kidnapped HVO officers from Novi Travnik. Now, if you are referring to the exchange, to the bit in which I participated in, that's a different matter. However, I would like to point out that the people in charge of that exchange were the European monitors. They were the ones who organised and executed that exchange. Your Honour, could you please be more specific and tell me, did you have in mind whether I knew Mr. Baggesen when I went to Ravno Rostovo with Mr. Juan Valentino? Or were you perhaps referring to the exchange itself, which took place much later? The exchange that I participated in did not take place in Ravno Rostovo, and I testified in detail about this. I don't know whether this was your question or it was misinterpreted by the interpreter. So could you please clarify, and let us make sure that we are keeping these things separate. The trip to Ravno Rostovo and the exchange of the HVO officers. So please, clarify which of these two instances do you want me to testify about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I wasn't yet so far that I could put you questions. But I said you visited Ravno Rostovo; you inspected the place, and you found no HVO officers. And I suggested to you that one of the members of the European observers, European monitors, although I did not say, that was a certain person called Lars Baggesen who has been here and has told exactly the same story as you did.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very glad, Your Honour, that Mr. Lars Baggesen gave the same story as I'm telling you now. All I'm saying is that the head of the delegation was Mr. Juan Valentino.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So we have no disagreement there. I'm glad to hear that you remember Mr. Lars Baggesen also as being one of the persons who accompanied -- who went together to the hotel and came back. He also told us an interesting detail about what happened after you visited the place. He told us that you all went to report your findings of your visit to an HVO commander and that when you were there, the military police of the HVO came in and wanted to arrest you personally. And this was apparently quite a row ending with the fact that the military police of the HVO arrested all of you, the whole delegation. And as he said, only after Blaskic had ordered our release could we leave the place. Is that also something that you remember?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remember those events very well. However, I disagree with Mr. Lars Baggesen on one issue. I know that Blaskic was requested to issue an order to the military police commander to release us. However, at Tihomir Blaskic's request, the permission was not granted. I said that our release was made possible on the basis of consent given by somebody above Mr. Blaskic, not Mr. Blaskic. So this is where Mr. Lars Baggesen and I differ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right. I would now like to show you a document that has the Exhibit Number P541. For those present, I may ask that there are three other documents that are related to the same topic, and that is P660, P461, and P409. I only want to discuss the Document P541. Have you got them? As you may note, these are two letters. The document on top is a letter of 3 April 1993. And it says below, but this is barely visible. It mentions the name of Tihomir Blaskic. Or the upper part of the letters "Tihomir Blaskic." Do you see that on page 2 -- page 1? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Is that also his signature? You said yesterday that you had seen few orders of Blaskic, but are you familiar with his signature?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot recognise Blaskic's signature. I can't do that with any great certainty. In addition to that, I see here in front of the word "commander" the word "for." Therefore, I assume that somebody signed it for Colonel Blaskic. I'm not an expert in recognising signatures. Your Honour, I cannot give you a comment concerning this. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You're right. It's -- it says "for Blaskic." The second document which is behind it is a letter of the 2nd of April. And if you look on the bottom, there is a stamp -- there is the typed name "Enver Hadzihasanovic," and there is a signature. Is that also a signature of the commander of the 3rd Corps? Again, I must say we have to deal with copies at the moment.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I recognise here only the beginning part of the signature, only the first part of the signature, based on what I know, and I've already stated that I could recognise the signature of my commander quite well. I don't see the second part of the signature, at least not in the document that I have in front of me. It is illegible. I don't see the entire signature. Therefore, I cannot confirm with full certainty that this indeed is the signature of my commander, General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I think it's better, then, to have the original document, and maybe the Prosecutor could provide us with that document, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, this is an exchange of letter. One letter has been written on the 2nd of April 1993. It comes from the 3rd Corps command apparently. And the other letter is of 3 April, and that is a response to the letter of 2 April, and also to another letter that doesn't matter at the moment. I would like you to have a look at the letter of the 2nd of April. That is the letter from the 3rd Corps command. May I ask you to read it in its entirety, and take your time and make it clear when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is very difficult for me to read this letter. I can't read the first part of the letter. Could I please see the original. If you ask me to read the entire text, that must mean that you are going to put questions to me about the whole document. So I would really need to see the original of the document, not because of the signature, but because of the text itself. It is quite a strain on my eyes. There have been a lot of poorly legible documents here, and I'm doing may best to answer all of your questions. Based on what I saw and what I experienced, and based on my own opinion about certain documents shown to me. Therefore, Your Honour, I would kindly ask at least for a better copy. It doesn't have to be the original, but at least a copy that is more legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid my copy is as bad as yours. But I can lend you my copy. And if that is not sufficient, then we would absolutely have to have the original.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same, Your Honour. Also very difficult to read. Perhaps, if you agree, I can read only portions of this letter, because this is quite a strain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break, and during the break -- but maybe Judge Swart could tell us the numbers of other documents where we might need the originals as well. No. Well, during the break, I'd like the Prosecution to try and find these documents, these two documents. It's 5.00. So we'll resume at 25 past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're waiting for the accused to come in. The Prosecution has found the originals, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have, Mr. President, obtained the best copies that we have from the evidence unit. Unfortunately, they are not the originals but are photocopies of the originals. But again, this is the best that we have in the Tribunal. And again, I did show those to the Defence counsel during the break. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to try using these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Witness, you were given two new photocopies, still not the original unfortunately. They are a little bit better to read, but it does not make an enormous difference, I think. Are you better able to read the documents, or do you still say "I cannot really read." If you say you cannot read, we might have to stop putting questions on the documents.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this copy is somewhat better than the previous one; however, it is still very difficult to read the first part of the document. If you want me to, I can read only the bits that are legible. However, I don't know whether based on that I will be able to answer your questions. It is up to you to decide. But there are portions that are barely legible, and I don't know if I will be able to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, let's have a try then. Read it very slowly, very carefully, read it again. If you are not able to understand the text and if you say, well, I can't really get what is in the letter, we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do my best to read the portions that are legible. I don't know whether you will be able to put together the entire picture based on what I read out. But I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Before we start doing that, it is enough to try or to try to read the letter of the 2nd of April, not the Blaskic letter, which is a response or seems to be a response to the document dated 2 April. Before you read, is the signature of the person who wrote the letter, is it more clear than the old copy you had?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It is identical to the signature on the previous copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So we still can't say with certainty whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not entirely certain as to whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right, then. Start to read, please, and take your time. I would propose you to read it first for yourself. And then if you think you're ready, then you may read it aloud for us, or we'll find a way to discuss further.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' request: Could we also have a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have read all that was legible in this document, all that was clearly legible. And I can understand most of what is written. If you want me, I can read it through so that you can check whether I'm reading correctly or whether the translation into English is accurate. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let's first run through it together, and then I'll ask you to comment on specific parts of the letter. I think at the fourth linea of the text, there is mention of an event on the 31st of March. Do you see that line? Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see, Your Honour. And I see the date, 31st March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What the letter is saying, that on the 31st of March at the HVO checkpoint at a certain road junction, members of the HVO police stopped a vehicle with foreign nationals. "Members of the BH Army," it says. Is that also what your text is saying? This is my translation, at least the translation I have.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see the reference to the members of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And then it goes on immediately after the vehicle was stopped, the foreign nationals were beaten on the spot with rifle butts and then taken to prison, most probably in Busovaca. Can you read that also in your text?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a word before "members of the BH Army" that I cannot make out. And below, I can read "instances when foreign nationals were stopped, beaten with rifles" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- "after which they were taken to prison. Most probably in..." I can't make out the following word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: We may be now in different parts of the letter. I'm not sure. We are in the part of the letter that mentions the date of the 31st of March 1993. You have that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I noticed that. And I read that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And what is the word you cannot read in that part of this letter?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the date and the indication of time. "Of 31st March 1993 when around 1700 hours" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- "at," it says "HVO," "at the Vitez-Travnik-Novi Travnik Road junction, members of the HVO stopped a vehicle in which there were foreign nationals." And then there is a word I can't make out. "Members of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The words at the left-hand side of the text are hardly readable, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I see your problem, yes. And the next sentence after the word "Armija RBiH."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the words "Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," I can make out some words, can't make out the others. "After being stopped, foreign nationals were physically beaten on the spot with" - a word I can't make out - "rifles, after which they were taken to prison, most probably in," and then a word I can't make out followed by a full stop. The text goes on. I can make out that it's some day in April 1993. "One of the three foreign nationals who were" - illegible word "at the checkpoint, was found killed in the area between Zabilje village and" the other name I can't make out, followed by a full stop. Then there is also an illegible bit, followed by the word "two foreign nationals, still nothing is" - and then I can't make out the word that follows. Full stop. The first word again is illegible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Maybe we will stop here for a moment, if I may interrupt you. Let me check whether we have the same idea of the content. I would summarise this by saying on the 31st of March some foreigners have been arrested at a checkpoint near a junction by the HVO police. And after their arrest, or after the car or the vehicle was stopped, these foreign nationals were beaten and brought to, probably, Busovaca. And on the 1st of April, one of the three foreign nationals was found dead or murdered at a certain place. Do we agree on that summary of the...?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with you on the summary of this passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, as you yourself read out, the first linea that you have read speaks about members of the BH Army. The other two lineas that we have read speak about foreign nationals. If you now turn to the top of the document, the head of the letter, could you read that. I think that is better readable than the rest of the text.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read, Your Honour, this first passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Could you read the top of the letter before the real text begins. I mean, read to us.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first word is not very legible. "Behaviour of HVO members," or rather "treatment by HVO members of foreign nationals, members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." It probably says "violent treatment by HVO members of foreign nationals who were volunteers in the BH Army." That's how I read this part of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's also how I would read it. Now, maybe it is too much asking to go to through the whole letter in view of the fact that you have difficulties in reading it. But I draw your attention to the fact that we have now together looked at two parts of the letter saying foreign nationals, volunteers in the BH Army. That's why I showed the letter to you. Could you comment on these expressions. If a letter says "foreign nationals, volunteers in the BH Army" or "foreign nationals, members of the BH Army," or uses other phrases in the same sense, what is your association with that? What -- how do we have to understand that as a reader of this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall interpret this document the way I understood it, and the way I partially read it. I completely understand the thrust of your question based on the passages we read together. You seem to be drawing my attention to the reference to "foreign nationals, volunteers in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." In the text below, it says that part of those foreigners, some of those foreigners were members of the BH Army. I have said, Your Honour, that we in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have a great many foreign nationals. Those are men who were not nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In some locations, in fact, we have a whole brigade of men who are not nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were nationals of other republics of the former Yugoslavia who came from other parts of foreign Yugoslavia, and they still do not have the nationality of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When it says "foreign nationals" here, it is not specified which nationality they have, from which country they are. So when it says that they were volunteers or members in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is not quite specific, even if it just says that they were foreign nationals. We had people from Slovenia, Sandzak, even Albanians, Macedonia. Most of those men later, after the war, returned to their original states. I have said previously in my testimony that we have a great number of men who came to Bosnia and Herzegovina at the beginning of the war, and in various capacities they joined up to offer armed resistance, armed resistance to the aggressor. Reference is made here to various forms of resistance to the aggressor. That can involve also humanitarian and other work in war-afflicted areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I cannot interpret this document otherwise. So mention is made of foreign nationals, some of which even remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I know of some cases of men from Kosovo who after the war sought nationality of Bosnia and Herzegovina and were granted nationality. I know men from Slovenia who later requested citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina and received it. All of them were also foreign nationals who joined up. It says it's true at some point from Europe and the world. It doesn't say exactly which countries, what kind of foreigners. It only says "foreign nationals."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, it doesn't specify what kind of nationals these persons are. They may also be former fellow countrymen who acquired a different nationality than the Bosnian nationality. That's right. I'm going to show you a related document now. That is P461. The 12th of April. I'm happy to say that the copy is better than the other copy. If we look together through the document, we see on the left top a mention of the 7th Muslim Brigade. There's a date, 12th of April. And at the bottom of the second page, we see a stamp. We see a name, Ahmet Adilovic, and a signature. Do you happen to know the signature of Ahmet Adilovic? Could you say this is, in fact, his signature?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot confirm that this is Ahmet Adilovic's signature. I have never seen his signature. Even if I had seen it, it would be difficult for me to confirm because as I said, I'm not an expert. Maybe the signature should be subjected to proper expertise. I told you that I can recognise the signature of my commander because it is peculiar, but this one I can't. I see that this man is assistant commander for morale, propaganda, and military affairs. I cannot, Your Honour, confirm that this is Mr. Ahmet Adilovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I take that into account, General. Would you say on the face of the letter that this is a document of the 3rd Corps or of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I've just read allows me to concur with you that, yes, this document originates from the 7th Muslim Brigade, 3rd Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... and that may allow me to go on then. Could you read the top of the letter, the two lines in capitals.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm having problems again with interpretation. I didn't say that I recognise the document of the 7th Muslim Brigade and that I can confirm that this is the document of the 7th Muslim Brigade. I'm not stating that, Your Honour. All I'm saying is that this is what the document reads. This is what is stated in this document. So there is probability that this document is indeed a document of the 7th Muslim Brigade. This is what is stated in the heading. However, I cannot confirm that this document is indeed a document from the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I think I'll stop questioning you at this moment. I think if you can not confirm this is of the 7th Brigade, I don't want to discuss the content with you. All right. So these were my questions. Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Judge has a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a few questions regarding the follow up of orders and the addressees of the investigation reports. But before I put my question, I have a few questions regarding your relationship with General Hadzihasanovic. How would you characterise your relationship with him? I mean, working relationship.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm a soldier. And if I'm to analyse the relations between us as soldiers, then those relations were proper and fair. My commander treated me properly, and I was content with the relations we had and with the way my superior officer treated me. I don't know whether my superior officer was content with my attitude towards him. However, in the military sense, I was happy and satisfied with our relations. Our relations were most proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before talking about the subordinate units, were you consulted as number two in the corps by the commander of the corps? When they would send orders to troops, to subordinate units, would they consult with you because you were the number two man?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were such cases. I cannot claim that he consulted me concerning the use of all units. However, there were such discussions. And occasionally, the commander would ask me what I thought of the combat activity of a certain unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it happen that you took decisions on your own, alone, when he wasn't there or when he wasn't at his duty station? Would you take decisions, alone, without him knowing about them?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never wanted to issue a decision on the use of units without prior consultation with the commander. However, I cannot exclude the possibility that there had been such cases, albeit at a low, tactical level. As far as I can remember, I never made a decision to use a unit at the brigade level without prior consultation with the command and the commander. I never made such decisions or orders on the use of a brigade. It is possible that there were cases where a unit was put in use when the commander was absent and such unit was perhaps used at a tactical level for defence actions. However, I never issued decisions on using units for other activity without consulting commander. I never issued orders for units to be used for offensive action without prior consultation with the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you aware of all the orders issued by the general?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of all of the orders issued and signed by the commander, General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to you, should a general know of everything happening in his area of responsibility? What do you think? Should he know about everything and anything happening in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understood your question. However, I need to clarify. It depends on the position held by the general within the command and control system. Your Honour, not all of the generals have to be aware of the combat activity. If you were referring to me as deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, then that's an entirely different matter, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to speak to you about the knowledge a commander has as to crimes committed by his subordinates. How is he made aware of them, of crimes committed by his subordinates? How? Through reports? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are several ways of informing the commander. The most proper way is by way of a report sent by a subordinate unit to the commander informing him that in the territory where that subordinate unit is deployed, a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what do you do if you receive such a report?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to remind you I do not wish to repeat myself. But we are now referring only to the crimes committed by the members of the BH Army. If we are clear on this, then, yes, I'm prepared to proceed with my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave extensive evidence concerning this, but let me remind you. When it is revealed that there had been a war crime, then Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there are organs within the units which start proceedings. They launch investigation, and then further proceedings against the soldiers who committed that crime. If the crime was committed in one of the units, then it is up to the military police of that unit to commence proceedings to initiate an investigation for the crime committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us assume that you received a report stating that there was some looting or fire. What do you do? I know that you initiate an investigation. You issue orders. We have a lot of orders among our documents, orders issued by the general. So he makes sure that an investigation is initiated, so he issues orders. Who does he issue the orders to, to subordinate units, for measures to be taken? Just correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon learning of an act that was committed, depending on where a crime was committed, the proceedings are initiated by the military police. The commander should order the military police to initiate proceedings for the crime committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he does send orders to the military police?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, to initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he sends orders to the units regarding individuals who looted or burnt places, what do the units do? I'm not yet speaking of the military police. What I have in mind is the units.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have police in units at the level of the brigade. We have military police at the level of the corps. I've already said that some brigades had military police units at the level of a company or at the level of a platoon. At the corps level, military police is organised in battalions. Therefore, the organs within the police are responsible for writing criminal reports and forwarding them to the prosecutor. And the perpetrators of crimes are tried by military courts. And this is a court that is outside of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the military police send them also a report, or does the police send the outcome of the investigation directly to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police sends it directly to the military prosecutor and informs the commander that a criminal report had been filled against the particular person. However, this is not done for individual cases. It is done for a certain period of time, unless a terrible, very grave crime had been committed in which case the police might decide to inform the commander immediately, without waiting for other crimes. But in principle, all of this is sent to the military prosecutor, and then forwarded to the military courts. And the commander is briefed about this on a monthly basis, or perhaps on a yearly basis. I also heard that occasionally, the commander of the corps was informed on a yearly basis. However, there could also be the cases where the commander was informed on a daily basis about the number of crimes committed in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the corps commander directly give the case or mention the case to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no knowledge of that. I know that at the level of the corps, there was a team of professionals who were supposed to prepare the material needed for filing criminal reports. I have no expertise in this field, Your Honour, so this is very difficult for me to explain the system to you. Within the 3rd Corps, there were special organs in charge of legal matters. This is a very important role played by lawyers who have to have proper legal qualification in order to carry out these duties. We had a person who was an expert within the 3rd Corps and who gave expert advice to the commander. Your Honours, I was not qualified in this field; therefore, I could give no advice to the commander regarding these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the military police investigating a case will send the report to the prosecutor, but will also send the report to the commander. Is that right? To inform the commander so that the commander knows about it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot clarify this to you in professional terms. I told you that commander would normally receive information about the number of crimes committed. Now, I cannot claim that commander would also receive the names of the perpetrators. I am sure that the military courts and military prosecutor received much more specific information as to the crimes and the perpetrators. I had occasion to see documents referring to NN persons, meaning persons whose identity was not known. And even in those cases where the perpetrators' identity was not known, the military police would initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which steps could you take, if any, if a subordinate of yours committed a wrongdoing, crime? Would you sue? Would you initiate legal action? Would that be person be relieved of their duty? I don't know. What steps, if any, did you take or would you take?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to any crime committed by a member of the BH Army, upon learning of that crime, the corps command or the command over a lower subordinated unit would initiate proceedings. I don't know what was the gravity of the crimes committed. But if the court issued a judgement to remove that person from office or to strip them of their rank, then this is what was done. I simply don't know about that, Your Honours. It is very difficult for me to give an answer to that question because this is not the field of my expertise. This was not within my scope of authorities. I'm simply giving you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If soldiers violated humanitarian, international law, can you confirm that all soldiers in that situation were prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the cases that we learned about, yes, I can confirm you that. However, as I told you here during my testimony, I do not exclude the possibility that there were cases when a BH Army member committed a crime but we did not learn about that. Only in those cases where we learned about that fact or had grounds to suspect that a member of the BH Army had committed a crime did we initiate the proceedings that I've described to you. So it does not necessarily have to be a situation where we know for sure that a member of the BH Army committed a crime. We could just have grounds to suspect that he committed a crime, and that would be sufficient to initiate criminal proceedings. And then in the course of those proceedings, it would be proven whether that member had indeed committed a crime or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking you to remember how many reports mentioned people, individuals who were prosecuted, reports that you did see and read.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have seen documents here indicating that there were reports mentioning hundreds of members of the BH Army in a certain period of time. I saw a document here stating that there were over 1.000 criminal reports filed against perpetrators who were members of the BH Army. Therefore, this is a report pertaining to just one area, the area of Travnik. If we were to put all the territory together, then I'm sure that the number would be in several thousands of criminal reports filed for crimes.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you want me to read the first word so that we can be sure that I'm reading the part that you want me to read? The first word in that paragraph is "I emphasise." This is the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall read that now. "I emphasise: Looting and crime dominate. Soldiers from the 'positions' are carrying bags full of goods through Zenica, and I have received information some of them refuse to go to positions unless there is something to loot." And then in parentheses, the 309th Mountain Brigade. "The police of some other brigades continue arresting and beating up civilians in basements. The Ministry of the Interior and the Security Services Centre and the 3rd Corps Security Service do not cooperate at all as was seen by Mr. Ganic during his meeting held at the 3rd Corps on the 15th of May 1993. Based on the above, I ask that you respond to this urgently as the personnel changes in the leadership of the 3rd Corps are needed. I have specific suggestions regarding this. I have asked from the commander of the 3rd Corps to replace the assistants for morale, security, and organisational and mobilisation and personnel issues, but there has been no response from him. "Together with Karic and Siber, please appoint to the joint command someone like Karisik, Vranj, and Najetovic instead of Merdan because Merdan is a member of the 3rd Corps and because of what was said about Merdan in the upper portion of this letter. "Best regards, Deputy Commander Stipan Siber."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is as follows: Are you able to state the grounds which prompted the deputy headquarters or staff, Commander General Siber, to ask for a change in the personnel in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot give you my comments on this document as a person who has just had occasion to read it. This document is outside of the system of control and command of the 3rd Corps. This is an expression of cooperation of the deputy commander, the supreme command, and the chief of staff. That's not at the level of the 3rd Corps, although I am not really supposed to comment on documents issued by the supreme command. But if you want me to, I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander recalls a number of arrests in this document, arrests of civilians, and he talks about basements, who were beaten up. Do you have any comments about this?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know in which way Mr. Stipan Siber got hold of this information. He probably had some information and was informing his commander accordingly; namely, the head of the supreme command. But I cannot explain where he found information that would justify this report. I really cannot explain that. I don't know where he got this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you yourself, as the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, were you not aware of these arrests and of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, whenever I was aware that a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did something like that, I wrote a report. And I said already that members of the BH Army who were responsible for such things and who were known to have done such things were subjected to appropriate measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If soldiers were arrested, why would General Siber have written that? Why would he have asked for personnel changes within the 3rd Corps in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only venture an opinion. Maybe Mr. Stipan Siber thought these people were the most responsible for what was going on, namely that civilians were being arrested, beaten in basements, et cetera. And maybe he thought if these people were replaced, these things would no longer go on. And that's why he's asking for these replacements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you please give the witness Exhibit Number P771. Can you tell us who signed this document. Who signed this report?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can make out that the president of the court was Mrs. Zijada Alihodzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please read the third paragraph from the end dealing with the case of members of the army.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Regarding the members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to the records of the court, there was no prosecution, neither for the period for which the query is made or for the entire duration of this court."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to benefit from your comments about this matter.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no comment. This was written by the president of the court. I cannot comment. I really have no comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the members of the army that had committed crimes and offences were prosecuted. Isn't that contradictory with what is stated by the president of the tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it says "cantonal court in Zenica." I was referring to the military court that operated during the war. I cannot really say whether reports were obtained also from military courts that were active during the war. But I have seen documents here that indicate that there were indeed prosecutions initiated for specific crimes. And the person who instituted criminal proceedings was signed below these documents. I see there the president of this court, Mrs. Zijada Alihodzic, is in a way denying this, saying the contrary. But I really cannot comment upon documents from the court. I'm afraid I would make another slip. It's really difficult for me to comment on documents of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 20 to 7.00. Does the Prosecutor want to use these 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, let me turn to the Defence counsel. We have 20 more minutes. Of course, we still have tomorrow morning. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, following a very, very long day, I would suggest that we break for today. And as for the additional questions by the Defence, they will take about four hours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, tomorrow we will finish at quarter to 2.00, on the dot. Therefore, I would like to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will have very few questions. No longer than 15 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 15 minutes. And four hours, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I said four hours, what I meant, and maybe I did not express myself clearly enough, what I meant is that the normal session, from 9.00 to 1.45 would be enough for the questions for both accused. Of course, if our colleague had asked for one hour, we would have only have used three hours. But we will not go beyond the hearing as it was set for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try to avoid any confusion as far as the documents are concerned. Now, about the admission of documents. Last time I said that the Defence was going to prepare a table, and then we would deal with that matter when we come back in January because we won't have enough time to deal with that tomorrow. In the same way, the lawyers of General Kubura submitted two documents, two documents. As for the Prosecution, if I remember rightly, there was one map -- no, two maps. That map over there, and we have to make sure that it doesn't disappear during the break. So we have two maps, and the two documents I mentioned, and another series of documents. So maybe as for the maps, we could solve and deal with that immediately. Maybe it's a good idea not to wait for next year in order to deal with the maps. Okay, the maps. Does the Defence have anything to say about the maps? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have any comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis. Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we offered only two documents, we would like to tender them as Defence exhibits because there are very few, and we can handle the issue immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, what do you have to say about the two documents submitted by Mr. Kubura's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, we need four numbers, four exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will start with the documents submitted by General Kubura's Defence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Two documents, the first one dated 6 August 1993, it will receive Exhibit Number DK25. And the English version will be DK25/E. The second document submitted by Kubura's Defence is dated 11 December 1992. The Exhibit Number will be DK26. The English version will be DK26/E. Now, as for the exhibits submitted by the Prosecution, the first map is the larger map that was used and that had already received a number for identification purposes under the number P938/ID. The final number will be P938. As for the map used with Witness Merdan with a scale of 1 to 25.000 with the date of 17/11/2004, its Exhibit Number will be P939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's still one document we need to deal with following the comments made by the Defence about -- related to a problem in the interpretation of a specific sentence, of the translation of a sentence in one document. We requested a translation that you received, both the Defence and the Prosecution. I'm turning to the Defence. Do you wish this document to be admitted, or to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objection to the translation we received in English and in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to the Prosecution about that specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, is this the document that we received a revised translation from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's Document P429.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no objection to the revised version being substituted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges will take a decision immediately to decide whether it's going to be a Chamber exhibit number or Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have decided to give this document a Chamber exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Exhibit Number will be C3. It's the third document submitted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a copy of the document? Okay. So that's that with this document. And we requested another document, and it will probably become Exhibit C4. We have ten minutes left. Are there any comments you would like to make? Well, we're probably going to be short with time tomorrow. As you know, we'll resume work in January on Monday, the 10th of January. I'm turning to the Registrar to confirm it. Yes, we'll start at 2.15, if I remember correctly. And as far as I know, no list of witnesses has yet been submitted. I'm speaking to the Defence here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will submit our list for the first set of hearings, from the 10th to the 16th, tomorrow because we have already made sure that these witnesses have passports and will receive visas. The second thing, and I need your leave for this, I already informed my colleagues from the Prosecution, additional questions following the Judges' questions will be handled by my colleague, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we had understood. We knew that it was going to be Mr. Bourgon because he stood up earlier on. Now, about the week of the 10th to the 16th, we'll be sitting in the afternoon. The Registrar will be able to confirm it. Yes, I believe we'll be sitting in the afternoon. The Queen of The Netherlands is going to host a function for the Judges, but I think it's in the morning. So the Judges will attend that function at the palace. We'll have enough time to come back for the hearing at a quarter past 2.00. Well, subject to additional information, I think it should be feasible for us to start the hearing at a quarter past 2.00. But don't worry, you will be kept informed about that. I do not have the date yet, but I think that we'll have an additional Judges' plenary because during the last plenary, while we were glad to listen to Mr. Bourgon's comments, we could not deal with the entire agenda. So there will be another plenary, and as soon as I know, I will tell you the day when we won't be sitting. But we might be sitting because the plenary might -- depending on whether the plenary will take place in the afternoon or the morning. As the schedule stands now, we should be sitting every day in January except for the 21st of January because I think it's a bank holiday. Well, I was not talking to fill in the time, but I needed to provide you with this information. Tomorrow, when we resume, I will give the floor to Mr. Bourgon who will be in charge of the additional questions. Then I will give the floor to Defence counsel who wish to take the floor, and that should take us to a quarter to 2.00, unless we finish earlier. Well, I wish you a very nice evening, a very good evening, because we've had a very long day. We are the only ones in the Tribunal to sit both in the morning and in the afternoon. General, you will have to come back. I thought that we would be able to complete your testimony today. But you'll have to come back tomorrow morning, but rest assured that we'll complete your testimony tomorrow at a quarter to 2.00. And you will be able to check with the relevant services of the Tribunal if you can take a plane back tomorrow afternoon. But rest assured that we will not be sitting beyond a quarter to 2.00. Please have a rest tonight because tomorrow you will have to answer the questions by the Defence. Thank you very much. See you tomorrow morning at 9.00.
